These examples illustrate the complex immunomodulatory influence of gut microbes: they can drive either pro‐ or anti‐tumor immune pathways in breast cancer, depending on the microbial composition and the host context. Although the lungs have their own microbiota, the gut microbiota can also influence lung cancer through systemic immune modulation. Microbe‐derived products from the gut can migrate via circulation to the lung and affect pulmonary immune homeostasis [70]. One way this manifests is in lung cancer patients' response to immunotherapy. Studies have shown that gut microbiota composition can predict which non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients respond to PD‐1/PD‐L1 inhibitors [7, 27]. Patients with higher baseline gut microbial diversity and the presence of certain commensals (like Akkermansia muciniphila, Alistipes putredinis, and Bifidobacterium longum ) had improved objective response rates and longer progression‐free survival on anti‐PD‐1 therapy [7, 25, 71, 72]. In contrast, those with a dominance of potentially pathogenic genera or low diversity tended to have poorer outcomes [73]. It is thought that a healthy microbiota “primes” the systemic immune system, for example by increasing the pool of effector CD8^{+} T cells or modulating myeloid cells in a way that enhances anti‐tumor immunity in the lung microenvironment [33, 74, 75]. In support of this, fecal transplant experiments from ICI‐responsive patients have improved lung tumor control in mouse models [76]. Conversely, antibiotic‐induced dysbiosis can have a detrimental effect on lung cancer therapy. In large patient cohorts, use of antibiotics around the start of ICI treatment was associated with significantly shorter survival in advanced NSCLC [7, 77]. A meta‐analysis of over 2000 NSCLC patients found that antibiotics reduced median progression‐free survival by ~1.2 months and overall survival by ~6–7 months [78, 79]. This suggests that the gut microbiota is integral to mounting an effective anti‐cancer immune response in the lungs, such that disrupting it impairs therapy efficacy. Preclinical studies offer mechanistic insight: one study found that certain gut bacteria induce the maturation of lung‐resident dendritic cells and promote Th1 cytokine production in the lung, thereby enhancing T cell‐mediated clearance of tumors [33, 80]. Without these microbial signals, lung tumors more easily escape immune surveillance. Even outside the context of immunotherapy, systemic inflammation driven by gut dysbiosis can contribute to lung carcinogenesis [81]. For example, circulating LPS from a leaky gut can activate lung macrophages and epithelial cells to produce pro‐tumor cytokines. In models of chemical carcinogenesis in the lung, GF or antibiotic‐treated mice (lacking normal gut flora) often show reduced tumor burden, consistent with a role for microbes in promoting tumorigenic inflammation [82, 83, 84, 85]. However, more research is needed to delineate specific gut–lung signaling metabolites in lung cancer. Emerging data suggest that metabolites like SCFAs might play a protective role by maintaining anti‐inflammatory regulatory cells in the lung, whereas others like certain bile acids or N‐nitroso compounds could potentially promote lung tumorigenesis. Overall, the gut microbiome appears to influence lung cancer initiation and progression largely via immune modulation. Melanoma has been at the forefront of microbiome–cancer research, largely because it was among the first diseases where gut microbial composition was linked to immunotherapy outcomes. Immune checkpoint blockade revolutionized melanoma treatment, but only a subset of patients derive durable benefit. Pioneering studies in 2015 and 2017 revealed that commensal gut bacteria can tip the scales of anti‐tumor immunity in melanoma [86]. Sivan et al. [6] famously demonstrated that mice with different gut microbiota had markedly different melanoma growth rates; cohousing or transferring stool between mice could transfer anti‐tumor immune phenotypes. They identified Bifidobacterium as a key genus in melanoma‐bearing mice improved tumor control as much as anti‐PD‐L1 therapy, and combined probiotic + anti‐PD‐L1 nearly eradicated tumors via enhanced dendritic cell and CD8^{+} T‐cell activity [73, 74, 87, 88]. Around the same time, Vétizou et al. found that Bacteroides species were required for optimal response to CTLA‐4 blockade in mice, as discussed earlier [33]. These discoveries in mice set the stage for human studies.

These examples illustrate the complex immunomodulatory influence of gut microbes: they can drive either pro‐ or anti‐tumor immune pathways in breast cancer, depending on the microbial composition and the host context. Although the lungs have their own microbiota, the gut microbiota can also influence lung cancer through systemic immune modulation. Microbe‐derived products from the gut can migrate via circulation to the lung and affect pulmonary immune homeostasis [70]. One way this manifests is in lung cancer patients' response to immunotherapy. Studies have shown that gut microbiota composition can predict which non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients respond to PD‐1/PD‐L1 inhibitors [7, 27]. Patients with higher baseline gut microbial diversity and the presence of certain commensals (like Akkermansia muciniphila, Alistipes putredinis, and Bifidobacterium longum ) had improved objective response rates and longer progression‐free survival on anti‐PD‐1 therapy [7, 25, 71, 72]. In contrast, those with a dominance of potentially pathogenic genera or low diversity tended to have poorer outcomes [73]. It is thought that a healthy microbiota “primes” the systemic immune system, for example by increasing the pool of effector CD8^{+} T cells or modulating myeloid cells in a way that enhances anti‐tumor immunity in the lung microenvironment [33, 74, 75]. In support of this, fecal transplant experiments from ICI‐responsive patients have improved lung tumor control in mouse models [76]. Conversely, antibiotic‐induced dysbiosis can have a detrimental effect on lung cancer therapy. In large patient cohorts, use of antibiotics around the start of ICI treatment was associated with significantly shorter survival in advanced NSCLC [7, 77]. A meta‐analysis of over 2000 NSCLC patients found that antibiotics reduced median progression‐free survival by ~1.2 months and overall survival by ~6–7 months [78, 79]. This suggests that the gut microbiota is integral to mounting an effective anti‐cancer immune response in the lungs, such that disrupting it impairs therapy efficacy. Preclinical studies offer mechanistic insight: one study found that certain gut bacteria induce the maturation of lung‐resident dendritic cells and promote Th1 cytokine production in the lung, thereby enhancing T cell‐mediated clearance of tumors [33, 80]. Without these microbial signals, lung tumors more easily escape immune surveillance. Even outside the context of immunotherapy, systemic inflammation driven by gut dysbiosis can contribute to lung carcinogenesis [81]. For example, circulating LPS from a leaky gut can activate lung macrophages and epithelial cells to produce pro‐tumor cytokines. In models of chemical carcinogenesis in the lung, GF or antibiotic‐treated mice (lacking normal gut flora) often show reduced tumor burden, consistent with a role for microbes in promoting tumorigenic inflammation [82, 83, 84, 85]. However, more research is needed to delineate specific gut–lung signaling metabolites in lung cancer. Emerging data suggest that metabolites like SCFAs might play a protective role by maintaining anti‐inflammatory regulatory cells in the lung, whereas others like certain bile acids or N‐nitroso compounds could potentially promote lung tumorigenesis. Overall, the gut microbiome appears to influence lung cancer initiation and progression largely via immune modulation. Melanoma has been at the forefront of microbiome–cancer research, largely because it was among the first diseases where gut microbial composition was linked to immunotherapy outcomes. Immune checkpoint blockade revolutionized melanoma treatment, but only a subset of patients derive durable benefit. Pioneering studies in 2015 and 2017 revealed that commensal gut bacteria can tip the scales of anti‐tumor immunity in melanoma [86]. Sivan et al. [6] famously demonstrated that mice with different gut microbiota had markedly different melanoma growth rates; cohousing or transferring stool between mice could transfer anti‐tumor immune phenotypes. They identified Bifidobacterium as a key genus in melanoma‐bearing mice improved tumor control as much as anti‐PD‐L1 therapy, and combined probiotic + anti‐PD‐L1 nearly eradicated tumors via enhanced dendritic cell and CD8^{+} T‐cell activity [73, 74, 87, 88]. Around the same time, Vétizou et al. found that Bacteroides species were required for optimal response to CTLA‐4 blockade in mice, as discussed earlier [33]. These discoveries in mice set the stage for human studies.

The aim of this systematic review was to identify all studies meeting the inclusion criteria, not to perform a quantitative synthesis of the results. RESULTS Included Articles Figure 1 illustrates the selection of the papers as a flow diagram. We found ten full-text papers and three abstracts that met the inclusion criteria. Five full-text articles27,30–33 and two abstracts34,35 analyzed the influence of antibiotics on ici efficacy; five full-text articles and one abstract evalu- ated the influence of the gm composition on ici efficacy; and three full-text articles explored the influence of the gm on iraes. Impact of Antibiotics on ICI Efficacy Table i summarizes the articles and abstracts that consid- ered the effect of antibiotics on ici efficacy. One study was prospective32; the remaining studies were retrospective. All publications presented results for two groups, an antibiotic- naïve (ABn) group and an antibiotic-treated [ABt (before or during receipt of icis)] group. Patients generally received oral antibiotics for common indications (dental, urinary, and pulmonary infections). Of the 997 patients included in the publications, 784 were in the ABn group, and 213 were in the ABt group. Most of the patients had nsclc (n = 561) or rcc (n = 338). All had received at least one of anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 or anti–ctla-4 therapy. Overall, use of antibiotics was associated with lower ici efficacy. In all publications, use of antibiotics in pa- tients with rcc negatively affected pfs (1.9–4.3 months in ABt patients vs. 7.4–8.1 months in ABn patients) and os (17.3–23.4 months in ABt patients vs. 27.9–30.6 months in ABn patients). The orr was also higher in ABn than in ABt patients (35%–78% vs. 13%–25% respectively)27,30,35. In all publications (except for two that lacked os data), use of antibiotics in patients with nsclc negatively affected os (4–7.9 months in ABt patients vs. 12.6–24.6 months in ABn patients); no differences in pfs (1.9–3.5 months vs. 2.8–3.8 months) or orr (25%–60% vs. 23%–63%) were observed27,30,34.

The presence of microbial interactions is a common phenomenon, so we explore the role of correlations between the bacterial and fungal kingdoms during ICI therapy. Overall, we found that in melanoma, the ecological network was more complex in responders (90 species, 2995 associations) compared to non-responders (90 species, 2149 associations) (Fig. 4a). In contrast, the trend is reversed in NSCLC, where responders exhibited 102 species and 807 associations, while non-responders had 92 species and 1170 associations (Fig. 4b). In addition to the robust connections among species within the kingdom, there are also substantial interactions between fungi and bacteria. Notably, responders demonstrated a higher degree of positive connection, regardless of whether they had NSCLC or melanoma (Fig. 4a, b). Consistently, a similar interaction pattern appears once the weak connection was eliminated in melanoma (|r|<0.55, Fig. 4c). After removing the weakly correlated microbial pairs, a trend was observed in NSCLC where the correlation was slightly stronger in responders than in non-responders (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, in melanoma responders, a higher proportion of fungal interkingdom interactions (Vanrija humicola, Tilletiopsis washingtonensis, Phanerodontia chrysosporium, Pyrenophora seminiperda) could be observed, while in NSCLC, the interactions among the Faecalibacterium (Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Faecalibacterium duncaniae, Faecalibaculum rodentium) were also more pronounced.Fig. 4Coabundance correlations among multi-kingdom species in responders and non-responders.a Summary of type of correlation and microbial pairs involving combined species related to ICI efficacy (Meta P < 0.1) from bacteria and fungi in melanoma; Only significant (FDR < 0.05) absolute correlations above 0.2 are shown; b Summary of type of correlation and microbial pairs involving combined species related to ICI efficacy (Meta P < 0.1) from bacteria and fungi in NSCLC; Only significant (FDR < 0.05) absolute correlations above 0.2 are shown; c Coabundance networks involving combined species related to ICI efficacy (Meta P < 0.1) from bacteria and fungi in melanoma; Only significant (FDR < 0.05) absolute correlations above 0.55 are shown; d Coabundance networks involving combined species related to ICI efficacy (Meta P < 0.1) from bacteria and fungi in NSCLC; Only significant (FDR < 0.05) absolute correlations above 0.55 are shown. However, in NSCLC, it was mostly found within the bacterial interkingdom. The cause of this difference cannot be ruled out as being due to the lower proportion of responders or the lower sequencing depth in NSCLC. Among these different microbial pairs, the correlation of responders was stronger than that of non-responders, whether in melanoma or in NSCLC (Supplementary Fig. 6b). 现有材料未提供关于抗生素暴露时机（治疗前 vs. 治疗后）对 ICI 疗效影响的系统 meta 分析证据。材料 P0118 和 P0612 指出，抗生素使用与 ICI 疗效降低相关，但仅笼统提及“ICI 治疗开始前后”（around the start of ICI treatment）或“治疗前或期间”（prior to or during anti-PD-1 therapy），并未区分具体时机的独立效应，也未提供针对该对比的 meta 分析数据。材料 P0188 专注于真菌标志物，不涉及抗生素研究。因此，无法从当前材料中得出关于暴露时机差异的具体结论。

现有证据表明抗生素暴露时机对ICI疗效的影响存在异质性，且不同肿瘤类型和给药模式下的表现不一致。在系统评价与Meta分析层面，时间窗口是解释疗效异质性的关键因素：在围治疗期（[-45, 45]天）内使用抗生素显著关联于总生存期（OS）恶化（β = 0.2192, p = 0.008），而治疗模式也起调节作用，联合治疗组中抗生素暴露显著降低OS（β = 0.2699, p = 0.002），但在未明确治疗模式的组别中观察到相反效应（β = -0.6152, p = 0.002）。具体到临床结局数据，回顾性研究汇总显示，在肾细胞癌（RCC）患者中，接受抗生素治疗（ABt）组的无进展生存期（PFS）和中位总生存期（OS）均显著短于未接受抗生素组（ABn），其中PFS分别为1.9–4.3个月对比7.4–8.1个月，OS分别为17.3–23.4个月对比27.9–30.6个月；客观缓解率（ORR）也较低（13%–25%对比35%–78%）。在非小细胞肺癌（NSCLC）患者中，抗生素使用同样显著缩短OS（4–7.9个月对比12.6–24.6个月），但部分研究显示PFS和ORR在两组间无显著差异。机制上，治疗前（如ICI前30天内）的广谱抗生素暴露被认为通过诱导肠道菌群失调削弱ICI疗效，而同期使用可能危害较小或无害，但这主要基于特定队列的观察，尚缺乏直接比较“治疗前”与“治疗后”暴露效应的独立验证。
